title: The Angelici and Laodicea: Theodoret on praying to angels in Phrygia and Pisidia
source_text: LXXXVI. Quaenam autem esset istorum pseudochristianorum, qui veteribus Angelici dicti sunt, erga Angelos Religio, colligere possumus ex Synodo Laodiceno: cujus reperitur hic Canon Codici Canonum Ecclesiae Universae insertus. Quod non oportet Christianos Ecclesiam Dei relinquere, & abire, & Angelos nominare, & Congregationes facere, quod est prohibitum. Quid vero sit, ex mente istius concilii, Angelos nominare, explicat Theodoretus in Epistolam ad Colossenses scribens, & locum illum quem urgemus exponens. Qui legem, inquit, defendebant, eos etiam ad Angelos colendos inducebant, dicentes legem fuisse per eos datam: Mansit autem perdiu hoc vitium in Phrygia & Pisidia. Proinde Synodus quae convenit apud Laodiceam Phrygiae, lege prohibuit ne precarentur Angelos. Et in hodiernum usque diem oratoria Sancti Michaelis apud illos illorumque finitimos videre est. Illi ergo humilitate nimirum ducti hoc fieri suadebant, dicentes universorum Deum nec cerni, nec attingi, nec comprehendi posse; & oportere per Angelos divinam sibi benevolentiam conciliare.
pass_a_gloss: But what the Religion toward Angels of those pseudo-Christians was, who by the ancients were called Angelici, we can gather from the Synod of Laodicea: of which this Canon is found inserted in the Code of Canons of the Universal Church. That Christians ought not to leave the Church of God, and go away, and name Angels, and make Congregations, which is forbidden. But what it is, in the mind of that council, to name Angels, Theodoret explains, writing on the Epistle to the Colossians, and expounding that place which we press. Those who defended the law, he says, led them also to worship Angels, saying that the law had been given through them: And this vice remained a very long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. Therefore the Synod which met at Laodicea of Phrygia prohibited by law that they pray to Angels. And to this present day oratories of Saint Michael are to be seen among them and their neighbors. They therefore, led namely by humility, urged that this be done, saying that the God of all things can neither be seen, nor touched, nor comprehended; and that it is fitting to win the divine goodwill for themselves through Angels.
pass_b_english: What kind of religion toward angels those false Christians had, whom the ancients called Angelici, we can learn from the Synod of Laodicea. One of its canons was taken into the Code of Canons of the Universal Church: "Christians ought not to forsake the Church of God and go off to name angels and hold assemblies, which is forbidden."

What "naming angels" meant to that council Theodoret explains in his commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, on the very passage we are pressing. "Those who defended the law," he says, "also led people to worship angels, saying that the law had been given through them. This vice lasted a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. That is why the synod that met at Laodicea in Phrygia forbade by law that anyone pray to angels. And to this day one can see oratories of Saint Michael among them and their neighbors. They urged this practice out of humility, as they claimed, saying that the God of all things cannot be seen or reached or grasped, and that we ought to win God's goodwill for ourselves through angels."

lemmas.gloss: the 'Angelics', a sect named for angel-worship

choices.english: out of humility, as they claimed
choices.why: Nimirum here is ironic; the English marks the humility as their own pretext.
